EUTv5BcTkZk.speaker: adnan
EUTv5BcTkZk.speaker_note: closes his own Ramadan values series and speaks of his years teaching in the city
EUTv5BcTkZk.title: Summary of Islamic Values
EUTv5BcTkZk.one_line: Closing the Ramadan values series: tawhid as the root of Islamic ethics, and the five domains of communal obligation for Muslims in the West.
EUTv5BcTkZk.summary: Closing his Ramadan series on values, the sheikh argues that the divine ethical code is the gem Muslims carry to the world, and that without it Islam is reduced to empty shells. Tawhid is not one value among others but the root of the whole system: because a wise, all-seeing Creator made the world with purpose, there is a moral code and accountability. The system protects itself only when kept whole; tolerating a little injustice or dishonesty makes it decay. Using the hadith that people are like metals and the example of Umar, he insists impeccable character with the basic obligations outweighs abundant worship mixed with corruption, and that the ummah's weakness reflects these lost basics. Masajid, schools and parents must teach people to prioritize values. He then restates the five domains of communal obligation he proposed four Ramadans earlier: education, mentorship across generations, unity through centralizing community wealth rather than competitive fundraising, organized outreach to unpracticing Muslims and non-Muslims, and advocacy that changes policy and narrative. Each person should choose one domain and commit to it, since masajid can only educate and mentor those who walk in; organizations should specialize and each carry part of the weight.

outline.heading: Ethics as the gift Muslims carry to the world
outline.gist: The divine moral code is the trust Muslims offer humanity; once lost, what remains of Islam is shells without essence. He cites the verse on the Lord's word completed in truth and justice.

outline.heading: Tawhid as the root of the moral system
outline.gist: Tawhid is not a value in the series but the source of all of them: a purposeful creation by an all-knowing Creator who holds people accountable requires a moral code.

outline.heading: A system that decays when one piece is neglected
outline.gist: Ethics anchored in tawhid never change, but allowing a little injustice or corruption in makes the whole system crumble.

outline.heading: People are like metals
outline.gist: The hadith that the best of people before Islam are the best in it once they understand: the deen came to bring an ethical system.

outline.heading: Umar's ethics carried into Islam
outline.gist: Umar came to Islam years late yet soared because his character was already sound; he would yield instantly to a woman's argument when told what Allah says.

outline.heading: Character outweighs abundant ritual
outline.gist: Those closest to the Prophet are the best in character; basic worship with impeccable ethics beats much worship with a little dishonesty or exploitation, and the righteous scholars were known for their truthfulness.

outline.heading: The ummah's state reflects its lost ethics
outline.gist: Muslims no longer stand for truth, rights and selflessness, and this loss explains the condition of the ummah; fiqh comes second to the ethical system.

outline.heading: Teaching people to prioritize values
outline.gist: Masajid, schools and parents must teach how to weigh values against each other, since the Prophet came to recalibrate and perfect good character.

outline.heading: Five domains of communal obligation in the West
outline.gist: He restates the framework he proposed four Ramadans earlier: every Muslim should engage in at least one domain, and each needs dedicated specialists.

outline.heading: First domain: education
outline.gist: Youth must learn every field and skill while deepening their Islamic literacy; the prophets left knowledge as their inheritance and current standards are far too low.

outline.heading: No one sits idle in our masjid
outline.gist: A travelling scholar sitting in a masjid in Turkey is told he must either teach or be taught, illustrating a culture of learning.

outline.heading: Second domain: mentorship
outline.gist: Mentorship needs life experience, not scholarship: every middle-aged person should check weekly on several younger people, as others once carried him.

outline.heading: Knowing the people you pray beside
outline.gist: Strong communities are interconnected; greet and learn the names of unfamiliar faces in the masjid so mentoring networks can form.

outline.heading: Third domain: unity through financial centralization
outline.gist: Of four ways a community unites (religious, political, social, financial leadership), only centralized wealth is realistic for Canadian Muslims.

outline.heading: Endowments instead of competitive fundraising
outline.gist: Organizations competing for donations is undignified; a pooled, professionally managed fund and endowments could buy centres, fund programs and pay imams properly.

outline.heading: Fourth domain: outreach to those outside the masjid
outline.gist: The same few thousand faces fill the masajid while most local Muslims and non-Muslims are never reached.

outline.heading: Organized dawah and care for converts
outline.gist: There are no funded, trained groups for outreach and converts are quickly lost; dawah must be organized rather than left to sporadic individual effort.

outline.heading: Fifth domain: advocacy
outline.gist: Changing policy and narrative, defending the oppressed and Palestine; the funding gap with pro-Zionist lobbying is shameful, and legislation like Bill C-9 shows the cost of silence.

outline.heading: Choose one domain and commit to it
outline.gist: Do not spread yourself thin; masajid can only educate and mentor those who walk in, so the other domains depend on community groups.

outline.heading: Specialize and shoulder part of the weight
outline.gist: Masajid should let people launch initiatives without claiming credit; organizations that each focus on one domain together lift the whole community.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.note: The divine moral code is the core of Islam and must be kept whole; neglecting one part makes the system decay.

wrHlbavpTvw.speaker_note: leads the night prayer and gives the reminder between rakaat; part of his Ramadan 2026 series
wrHlbavpTvw.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 29: Ninth Night of Tahajjud
wrHlbavpTvw.one_line: Between rakaat on the 29th night: seek forgiveness before dawn, never feel you have done enough, and carry that humility beyond Ramadan.
wrHlbavpTvw.summary: On the twenty-ninth night of Ramadan 2026, Sh. Adnan gives one short reminder between rakaat. As the month closes, he tells people not to expect to carry all of Ramadan forward, because that will not happen, but to keep some of it, such as a set time to rise and pray at night. He then reflects on how Allah describes the righteous as people who sleep little at night and seek forgiveness before dawn, and who are named together as patient, truthful, devout, generous and seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours. The immediate lesson is to use the last third of the night, the prime time for asking forgiveness. The deeper lesson is the mindset behind it: people with this much worship are not made arrogant by it, do not see themselves as better than other Muslims, and never think they have done enough. That humility and constant asking for forgiveness, he says, is the one thing he hopes everyone takes out of Ramadan, and he closes the reminder with the prophetic dua of one who admits he has wronged himself greatly and asks Allah alone to forgive him.

outline.heading: Opening
Interlude
Carry some of Ramadan forward, not all of it
outline.gist: As Ramadan ends he asks people to keep part of their night worship going, like a set time to rise and pray, knowing they will not keep the whole of it.

outline.heading: The righteous seek forgiveness before dawn
outline.gist: Allah describes the righteous as sleeping little and asking forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours; the immediate lesson is to use the last third of the night, a prime time for forgiveness.

outline.heading: Worship that does not breed arrogance
outline.gist: Allah mentions their seeking forgiveness alongside their patience, obedience and spending: all that worship does not make them think they are better than other Muslims.

outline.heading: Never feel you have done enough
outline.gist: They ask forgiveness at the most blessed time without thinking they have done enough; that mindset is what he hopes people carry out of Ramadan, sealed with the dua of one who has wronged himself.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro

themes.label: Tawbah: repentance and returning to Allah
themes.note: Seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours is the mark of the righteous, and the habit he most wants carried beyond Ramadan.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Great worship should not make a person feel superior to other Muslims or feel that he has done enough.

themes.label: Ramadan: preparation, fasting, making the most of it
themes.note: At the end of the month the goal is to carry part of its worship forward rather than lose all of it.

themes.label: Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance
themes.note: Keeping a regular time for night prayer and using the last third of the night.

quran.point: The righteous slept little at night and sought forgiveness before dawn.
Seeking forgiveness before dawn is listed together with patience, truthfulness, devotion and spending.

hadith.gist: The prophetic dua: My Lord, I have wronged myself greatly and none forgives sins but You, so grant me forgiveness from You and have mercy on me; You are the Forgiving, the Merciful.

maxims: Carry some of it forward, not the entire thing
takeaways: Keep a portion of Ramadan's night prayer after the month instead of dropping it all.
Use the last third of the night before Fajr to ask Allah for forgiveness.
Do not let your worship make you feel better than other Muslims.
Never feel you have done enough; ask forgiveness as someone in need of mercy.
Make the dua of admitting you have wronged yourself a regular habit.

14:21.ar: وَبَرَزُواْ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا فَقَالَ ٱلضُّعَفَٰٓؤُاْ لِلَّذِينَ ٱسۡتَكۡبَرُوٓاْ إِنَّا كُنَّا لَكُمۡ تَبَعࣰ ا فَهَلۡ أَنتُم مُّغۡنُونَ عَنَّا مِنۡ عَذَابِ ٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ قَالُواْ لَوۡ هَدَىٰنَا ٱللَّهُ لَهَدَيۡنَٰكُمۡۖ سَوَآءٌ عَلَيۡنَآ أَجَزِعۡنَآ أَمۡ صَبَرۡنَا مَا لَنَا مِن مَّحِيصࣲ‏
14:21.en: They all come forth unto their Lord. Then those who were despised say unto those who were scornful: We were unto you a following, can ye then avert from us aught of Allah's doom? They say: Had Allah guided us, we should have guided you. Whether we rage or patiently endure is (now) all one for us; we have no place of refuge

4:59.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ أَطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُواْ ٱلرَّسُولَ وَأُوْلِي ٱلۡأَمۡرِ مِنكُمۡۖ فَإِن تَنَٰزَعۡتُمۡ فِي شَيۡءࣲ فَرُدُّوهُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَٱلرَّسُولِ إِن كُنتُمۡ تُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِۚ ذَٰلِكَ خَيۡرࣱ وَأَحۡسَنُ تَأۡوِيلًا
4:59.en: O ye who believe! Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority; and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger if ye are (in truth) believers in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more seemly in the end

51:56.ar: وَمَا خَلَقۡتُ ٱلۡجِنَّ وَٱلۡإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعۡبُدُونِ
51:56.en: I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me

2:126.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ ٱجۡعَلۡ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا ءَامِنࣰ ا وَٱرۡزُقۡ أَهۡلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ مَنۡ ءَامَنَ مِنۡهُم بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِۚ قَالَ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُۥ قَلِيلࣰ ا ثُمَّ أَضۡطَرُّهُۥٓ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلنَّارِۖ وَبِئۡسَ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
2:126.en: And when Abraham prayed: My Lord! Make this a region of security and bestow upon its people fruits, such of them as believe in Allah and the Last Day, He answered: As for him who disbelieveth, I shall leave him in contentment for a while, then I shall compel him to the doom of Fire - a hapless journey's end

2:143.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلۡنَٰكُمۡ أُمَّةࣰ وَسَطࣰ ا لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ شَهِيدࣰ اۗ وَمَا جَعَلۡنَا ٱلۡقِبۡلَةَ ٱلَّتِي كُنتَ عَلَيۡهَآ إِلَّا لِنَعۡلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ ٱلرَّسُولَ مِمَّن يَنقَلِبُ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيۡهِۚ وَإِن كَانَتۡ لَكَبِيرَةً إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ هَدَى ٱللَّهُۗ وَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَٰنَكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِٱلنَّاسِ لَرَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
2:143.en: Thus We have appointed you a middle nation, that ye may be witnesses against mankind, and that the messenger may be a witness against you. And We appointed the qiblah which ye formerly observed only that We might know him who followeth the messenger, from him who turneth on his heels. In truth it was a hard (test) save for those whom Allah guided. But it was not Allah's purpose that your faith should be in vain, for Allah is Full of Pity, Merciful toward mankind

2:129.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱبۡعَثۡ فِيهِمۡ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
2:129.en: Our Lord! And raise up in their midst a messenger from among them who shall recite unto them Thy revelations, and shall instruct them in the Scripture and in wisdom and shall make them grow. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Mighty, Wise

FJ6vgK1gpDs.speaker: adnan
FJ6vgK1gpDs.speaker_note: final episode of his own seven-part series; speaks of growing up in Syria and working in a hospital
FJ6vgK1gpDs.title: The Philosophy of Islamic Thought #7: Political Systems and Governance in Islam
FJ6vgK1gpDs.one_line: Seven principles of Islamic governance, then the four classical questions on God, humanity, purpose and Islam's vision of a good world.
FJ6vgK1gpDs.summary: He argues that Islam gives political principles, a moral architecture, rather than a fixed state blueprint, and that no system survives without moral people running it. He sets out seven principles. Sovereignty belongs to Allah while agency belongs to people, so there is no obedience in disobedience and no hiding behind being a mere soldier, as Imam Ahmad told his jailer. Governance exists for justice; jurists preferred a just non-Muslim ruler to an unjust Muslim one. Consultation is obligatory and qualified voices should weigh more, in contrast to one-man cults of leadership like the Syria he grew up in. The ruler is a trustee whose legitimacy is conditional, as Abu Hanifa's defiance of al-Mansur showed. Law stands above personality, with independent scholars functioning like a judiciary, which is what Imam Ahmad's stand truly defended. Governance serves the higher objectives of the law. Finally, governance is an outcome built from the people upward, never imposed by coups or invasion, so legitimacy must precede enforcement. He then answers the classical questions: Allah as the one necessary source of reality, the human as a dignified, fallible trustee, life as a moral test judged by intention and accountability, and a utopia of security, provision, tawhid, repentance and moral example drawn from the prayers of Ibrahim and the Prophet.

outline.heading: Opening
Governance comes last, not first
outline.gist: Modern sects overrate the political dimension compared with what Islam emphasizes.

outline.heading: Principles, not a blueprint
outline.gist: As in fiqh, Islam gives load-bearing principles and leaves people to build structures suited to their time and place.

outline.heading: Only moral people can protect a system
outline.gist: A rigid system cannot stop corruption; a man without morals leading the strongest country shows that the morality of those governing matters most.

outline.heading: Abandoned principles and post-colonial dictatorships
outline.gist: Muslims set the principles aside, and colonial powers installed dictators, which is why many families emigrated.

outline.heading: Principle 1: sovereignty belongs to Allah, agency to people
outline.gist: Rulers govern in Allah's name over His land and people, organizing affairs in a way that pleases Him.

outline.heading: No cookie-cutter political system
outline.gist: Exporting one model everywhere is naive; systems must fit each people's history, norms and needs.

outline.heading: No obedience in disobedience of Allah
outline.gist: Being just a soldier is no excuse; the Quran shows the weak blaming the powerful and Allah rejecting the excuse.

outline.heading: Imam Ahmad's jailer: oppressor, not helper
outline.gist: A guard who lashes knowingly is an oppressor himself; even under threat you may not harm another.

outline.heading: The moral code, not policy, is the line
outline.gist: Taxes and penal timing are for scholars to weigh; Abu Bakr said obey me only while I obey Allah.

outline.heading: Principle 2: the purpose of governance is justice
outline.gist: Once oppression spreads, the oppressed side with any invader, which is why tyrannies fall.

outline.heading: A just non-Muslim ruler over an unjust Muslim one
outline.gist: Power is a test; al-Mawardi and Ibn Taymiyyah held that a ruler's justice benefits all while his piety benefits only him.

outline.heading: What justice protects
outline.gist: The khalifa is a public servant; justice means protecting life, property, dignity and freedom of thought, not sanctifying rulers.

outline.heading: Principle 3: consultation is obligatory
outline.gist: The Prophet and each caliph used different models of shura; what matters is that power is not held by one or a few.

outline.heading: Qualified voices should weigh more
outline.gist: Those who bind and loosen choose and judge leaders; equal votes push politicians to cater to the masses with spectacle.

outline.heading: Epistemic humility versus the cult of the leader
outline.gist: In Syria, North Korea and the Soviet Union one man was treated as all-wise; Islam is farthest from that.

outline.heading: Principle 4: the ruler is a trustee: Abu Hanifa and al-Mansur
outline.gist: Unlike divine-right kings, caliphs were stewards; Abu Hanifa refused to serve an oppressor, died in his prison and refused burial on seized land.

outline.heading: Conditional legitimacy and the overstated obedience verse
outline.gist: Unjust rulers must be removed, but carefully, avoiding chaos and worse bloodshed; rulers suppress this teaching.

outline.heading: Legitimacy is chosen, not mystical
outline.gist: Rulers are chosen by people and bound by the moral code, not crowned by any religious authority.

outline.heading: Principle 5: law over personality
outline.gist: Jurists acted as an independent judiciary, which is why Malik, Ahmad and al-Shafi'i were persecuted.

outline.heading: What Imam Ahmad really defended
outline.gist: Not mainly a creedal point but scholars' autonomy from the caliph; with Abu Bakr's stand on zakat, it protected the din.

outline.heading: Scholars must speak their minds
outline.gist: The qualified may be wrong; once a scholar speaks for rulers, Islam itself is turned against ordinary people.

outline.heading: An early separation of powers
outline.gist: Scholars interpreted, judges applied, rulers administered; a scholar's job is to hold politicians accountable, not cheer them.

outline.heading: Principle 6: the higher objectives of the law
outline.gist: Preserving religion, life, intellect, lineage and property are the metrics of legitimate governance, making politics goal-oriented.

outline.heading: Principle 7: governance is an outcome, built from below
outline.gist: The Prophet refused kingship in Mecca and built from the ground up; extremists invert the pyramid.

outline.heading: Coups and invasions do not work
outline.gist: Removing a tyrant by force brings years of bloodshed; the Arab uprisings of 2010 were suppressed by outside powers.

outline.heading: Legitimacy precedes enforcement
outline.gist: The West wants democracy only for itself; the law of Allah must be chosen by people, an ascending system of voluntary adherence.

outline.heading: Coercion only delays bloodshed
outline.gist: Even on consequentialist grounds imposed order fails, bottling anger until it explodes.

outline.heading: Summary of Islamic political theory
outline.gist: Theocentric, consultative, justice-driven, legally grounded with an independent court, welfare-oriented and legitimate before enforcing.

outline.heading: Its own paradigm, unlike Western or Chinese models
outline.gist: Admiring China's totalitarian model is folly; in Syria the leader's portrait was the most valuable thing in any shop.

outline.heading: The four classical questions and the flow of knowledge
outline.gist: Muslim scholars took a bird's-eye view early; Europe later built on translated Muslim works, part of a shared human relay of knowledge.

outline.heading: Who is the Creator
outline.gist: Allah is the one necessary, transcendent source of all reality; one origin means one set of laws, ethics and values.

outline.heading: Why this concept of God is unmatched
outline.gist: Every other concept bears a human fingerprint; Islam preserved this one, from which most of reality can be deduced.

outline.heading: What is a human being
outline.gist: A moral, rational, free and dignified creature, fallible, entrusted as steward: neither divine nor insignificant.

outline.heading: The purpose of existence: a moral test
outline.gist: Life is to know and worship Allah and align with His guidance; the test is of moral choices more than ritual precision.

outline.heading: The trolley problem and intention
outline.gist: Islam cares less about the answer than the reasoning behind it, and condemns overcomplicating simple cases to escape the right choice.

outline.heading: Accountability in the afterlife
outline.gist: Only knowing Allah sees your motives keeps morality honest; this cannot be separated from Islamic philosophy.

outline.heading: Islam's goals: awareness, transformation, stewardship, justice
outline.gist: Islam aims at ethical transformation of the self and protection of life, intellect, family, property and faith.

outline.heading: Utopia 1: the spread of security

outline.heading: Utopia 2: abundance of provision

outline.heading: Utopia 3: tawhid and established prayer

outline.heading: Utopia 4: accepting repentant sinners

outline.heading: Utopia 5: moral refinement as witnesses

outline.heading: Utopia 6: the sending of the final Messenger

outline.heading: One thread through every system
outline.gist: Moral, financial, social, psychological and political systems share one purpose: protecting individual and collective under a moral compass.

7_CcaX6yV2s.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Mursalat, Part 1: Verses 1-15
7_CcaX6yV2s.one_line: Al-Mursalat's oaths show everything in life leaves an impact, the Day is just as certain, and the deniers are those who knowingly refuse truth.
7_CcaX6yV2s.summary: Al-Mursalat closes the dawah cluster of Juz Tabarak, and after surahs that appealed to the intellect and to reward, it focuses on just punishment. Warning comes first because missing a warning is unforgivable, and justice requires consequences for both good and bad; he applies this to parenting and argues we understand things through their opposites. He reads the opening oaths as generic on purpose: whether winds or angels, everything sent brings good or harm, spreads it, makes a difference and leaves a reminder. Just as surely, what you are promised will happen, and no one can stay neutral, since not choosing is a choice. He then describes stars wiped out, the sky opened like a window and mountains destroyed in an instant, noting the passive voice tells you to focus on what you will witness. Even the messengers have an appointment to give account, some arriving with no followers at all, on the Day of Decision. The refrain 'woe that day to the deniers' leads to his main point: a mukadhdhib is not any disbeliever but someone who sees truth and refuses it. A Muslim never has to defend what is wrong, because he is Muslim since Islam is true. Admitting error is liberating, while defending sects, parties or opinions is exhausting.

outline.heading: Al-Mursalat: the third model of dawah
outline.gist: The cluster from Al-Mulk to Al-Mursalat is about representing Islam and calling to it. After Al-Qiyamah's appeal to the intellect and Al-Insan's to reward, Al-Mursalat focuses on just punishment and the reverence it should produce.

outline.heading: Interlude
Every surah is its own unit
outline.gist: Everyone should know the last juz by heart and understand it, since it holds the largest share of the Quran's 114 surahs. The longest and the shortest surah differ in size, but each is a complete unit delivering its own message, so none is unworthy of learning.

outline.heading: How Al-Qiyamah and Al-Insan made their case
outline.gist: Al-Qiyamah speaks to the conscience: does man think he will be left aimless, when he has insight over himself? Al-Insan speaks to the part of you that can rise above materialism: you worship One who has so much to offer and has promised it.

outline.heading: Warning comes before good news
outline.gist: The Prophet is often a warner before a bearer of glad tidings, because you would forgive someone who forgot to mention a reward but not one who failed to warn you of ruin. This is not sadism: once people can choose, justice needs consequences for both kinds of behaviour.

outline.heading: Parenting with rewards and consequences
outline.gist: Children who are rewarded for good but face no consequence for mistakes or bad manners grow into non-functional adults who keep getting themselves into trouble.

outline.heading: We understand things through their opposites
outline.gist: Every game has progress or death. Goodness, ease and love are only understood against evil, hardship and fear, and the easiest way to define something is to say what it excludes; hence the wisdom of having both reward and punishment.

outline.heading: The news shows why Hell must exist
outline.gist: Watching slaughter and mistreatment on the news, no one struggles to see why there is a Hell; without it there is no fairness. All we try to do is stay off the wrong side of that equation.

outline.heading: Allah's oaths carry their own lesson
outline.gist: He recites the opening verses. Human oaths are only a lead-in to the statement that follows, but every oath of Allah tells a story of its own, tied to the theme of the surah.

outline.heading: Swear only by Allah, and rarely
outline.gist: Scholars differ on how strictly swearing by other than Allah is forbidden; he advises avoiding it and keeping oaths for moments that truly need them, since overuse empties them of weight.

outline.heading: Sent with goodness, and sent as a storm
outline.gist: 'Urf shares its root with ma'ruf, what is known to be good. Most scholars say the verses mean winds and some say angels, but he holds the generic wording is deliberate. 'Asifat combines violence with movement, as in a storm.

outline.heading: Repeating the root means done to the full
outline.gist: When a verb's root is repeated as its object, it stresses that the action was done completely, every box checked and nothing half-done, like saying someone truly ate.

outline.heading: Spreading what they bring and making a real difference
outline.gist: Nashirat spread what they carry in the right way, and fariqat bring a decisive difference: what they do changes how things function, and goodness and storm produce very different results.

outline.heading: Every reminder either excuses or warns
outline.gist: They cast a reminder that either offers an excuse and encouragement or a warning. He does not name what is meant because it does not matter: everything in the world brings good or severe harm, spreads it, makes a difference and leaves a lesson to reflect on.

outline.heading: A constant process you are part of
outline.gist: Health, wealth, disease and family all do the same. The participle forms show the sending never stops, and you yourself become one of these forces, spreading good, evil or something worthless like dead leaves. The oaths tell a full story of how the world moves.

outline.heading: What you are promised will surely happen
outline.gist: The answer to the oaths: just as no one can deny that everything sent leaves a ripple effect, the promised Day is equally real. Everyone makes an impact and leaves a legacy.

outline.heading: No neutrality: not choosing is a choice
outline.gist: You cannot step out of the story. Deciding not to get involved is itself a choice with consequences; you are not a rock but a human being in the middle of the arena, so choose your side and the impact you leave.

outline.heading: Rain or sand: the oaths applied
outline.gist: Winds bring rain that greens the land or sand that kills it; angels bring goodness or punishment; each disperses what it brought and leaves a reminder. Since that first half cannot be refuted, neither can the promise.

outline.heading: Reciting verses 8-15: the doubled ya
outline.gist: In li-ayyi yawmin a doubled ya meets another ya, which the mouth resists, so the lower jaw has to move to bring both out clearly rather than running them together.

outline.heading: Stars obliterated, presence and effect
outline.gist: Tamasa removes both a thing's presence and its effect, like eyes wiped away so that sight is gone too; the stars will be removed in the same complete way.

outline.heading: The sky opened like a window
outline.gist: Furijat comes from the opening you watch through, as a television or phone is a window into elsewhere. The sky is a barrier hiding what lies beyond; it will tear open and show what the human mind is not ready to see.

outline.heading: Mountains blown away in an instant
outline.gist: Nasf is instant destruction, a word still used in warfare. Mountains are the stable rock you wake up to every day; having grown up beneath one in Syria, he describes how they become part of your identity.

outline.heading: The Prophet and the mountains of Madinah
outline.gist: Every mountain around Madinah had a name the Prophet knew, and he said Uhud loves us and we love it. People lived at the foot of mountains for water and for refuge from raids, and these are what vanish in a moment.

outline.heading: The passive voice: you will see
outline.gist: He does not say 'when I obliterate the stars' but 'when the stars are obliterated'. Do not worry about who or how; worry about what you will witness.

outline.heading: The messengers given their appointed time
outline.gist: Uqqitat comes from waqt: the messengers are given an appointment to appear and argue their cases. He counts these four short verses among the heaviest in the Quran.

outline.heading: Nuh presents his case
outline.gist: He recites Nuh's account of calling his people night and day, in public and in private, as the case Nuh will present. Many prophets whose stories we never heard will do the same.

outline.heading: A prophet who arrives alone
outline.gist: The Prophet saw prophets coming with a small group, with one or two men, and one with no one at all, not even family. The appointment asks whether you did your job and gave the effort needed, not how many followed.

outline.heading: Postponed to the Day of Decision
outline.gist: Ujjilat is postponement. Fasl is separation, as a classroom is a separated room: a day that divides right from wrong with no extensions, when every question is answered and every oppression meets justice.

outline.heading: Woe that day to the deniers
outline.gist: What will make you know that Day? Only what Allah tells us: it is certain. The one thing to know is repeated nine times in the surah: wayl, an inevitable punishment, for the mukadhdhibin, the term that unlocks the surah.

outline.heading: Kafir: a broad category only Allah judges
outline.gist: We know nothing of a given kafir's disbelief: whether he received the message, lived between prophets, made an ethical or theological error, or was too oppressed to ask questions; such people may well be forgiven. We wish Jannah for everyone and leave the outcome to Allah.

outline.heading: The mukadhdhib saw the truth and refused it
outline.gist: A mukadhdhib hears what clicks as true and says no, out of arrogance, fear or self-interest. Often it is the difficulty of admitting at forty or fifty that you have been wrong for decades.

outline.heading: Defending what is wrong enslaves you
outline.gist: A Muslim never has to defend a wrong. Defending one forces you to bend reality and spin narratives, which is exhausting, worsens anxiety and is a form of enslavement, as when people defend what their parents or tribe did.

outline.heading: I am Muslim because Islam is right
outline.gist: If the Most Merciful had a son, the Prophet would be first to worship: follow truth wherever it is. Tazkiyah is honesty with yourself, which releases pressure like a pressure cooker; learn until you are at peace with your faith instead of avoiding grey areas.

outline.heading: Small denials grow into the ultimate one
outline.gist: Defending a party, sect, organisation or one's own opinions are smaller forms of takdhib, and with time they lead to denying the ultimate truth. Deniers are lying to themselves, and simply admitting a mistake brings enormous relief.

outline.heading: No scholar, madhhab or agenda to defend
outline.gist: If he had to defend a teacher or madhhab at all costs he would end up bending the Quran to fit his box; scholars did much good and made mistakes, as he will. An agenda makes you hear only what suits you, which social media algorithms exploit.

outline.heading: Say the truth even when it is unpopular
outline.gist: Teaching is not the old Syrian TV request show that played whatever callers asked for. He says what is right and retracts when shown wrong; you sleep well even if you lose popularity, while the deniers face their worst day.

outline.heading: Preview: history, the universe and life
outline.gist: The next verses argue for Allah from history, the universe and life. Concluding there is no God from everything we observe means switching off logic for this one question.

themes.label: Truthfulness and honesty
themes.note: Follow the truth wherever it is; never defend what you know is wrong; admitting error is liberating and self-honesty is the core of tazkiyah.

themes.label: Atheism, doubt and responding to disbelief
themes.note: The deniers threatened in the surah are those who see truth and refuse it, unlike the broad category of kafir whose circumstances only Allah knows.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: Stars obliterated, sky opened, mountains destroyed, prophets summoned, and the decisive Day with no extensions.

themes.label: Justice and refusing oppression
themes.note: Justice requires consequences for both good and bad; seeing atrocities on the news makes the need for Hell obvious.

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Everything leaves an impact and a reminder; there is no neutrality, so choose the impact and legacy you leave.

themes.label: Stories of earlier prophets
themes.note: Prophets too are given an appointed time to account for their mission, some with no followers.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Children raised with rewards but no consequences become non-functional adults.

themes.label: Oaths, promises, trust and loyalty
themes.note: Avoid swearing by anything other than Allah and keep oaths for moments that truly need them.

themes.label: Atheism, doubt and responding to disbelief
themes.note: Concluding there is no God from everything we observe means turning off logic for one question.

62:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَوٰةِ مِن يَوۡمِ ٱلۡجُمُعَةِ فَٱسۡعَوۡاْ إِلَىٰ ذِكۡرِ ٱللَّهِ وَذَرُواْ ٱلۡبَيۡعَۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
62:9.en: O ye who believe! When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading. That is better for you if ye did but know

62:10.ar: فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةُ فَٱنتَشِرُواْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَٱبۡتَغُواْ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تُفۡلِحُونَ
62:10.en: And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much, that ye may be successful

62:11.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَوۡاْ تِجَٰرَةً أَوۡ لَهۡوًا ٱنفَضُّوٓاْ إِلَيۡهَا وَتَرَكُوكَ قَآئِمࣰ اۚ قُلۡ مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنَ ٱللَّهۡوِ وَمِنَ ٱلتِّجَٰرَةِۚ وَٱللَّهُ خَيۡرُ ٱلرَّٰزِقِينَ
62:11.en: But when they spy some merchandise or pastime they break away to it and leave thee standing. Say: That which Allah hath is better than pastime and than merchandise, and Allah is the Best of providers

uTHHc2emGb0.speaker_note: MWN Friday khutbah opening his 'Communal Covenant' series; reads the ten points from his own February 18, 2022 opening khutbah and mentions being paged from the hospital
uTHHc2emGb0.title: Our Communal Covenant: Our End of the Bargain
uTHHc2emGb0.one_line: Opening the covenant series, he re-reads the ten commitments his masjid made at its 2022 opening and promises to spell out the community's side in coming weeks.
uTHHc2emGb0.summary: After a sharp aside about texting during the khutbah, which is forbidden unless you are on call for lives, he reads from his phone the khutbah he gave when the centre opened on February 18, 2022. His argument is that Muslim communities run in circles because no memorandum of understanding exists between those who run masajid and those who attend them; both sides fail, and he has seen it in masajid worldwide since age five. The Prophet transformed a society in 23 years, and he secured a covenant with the Ansar before Madinah. Everyone must shoulder some weight according to their stage of life. He then reads his side: ten points covering balanced teaching with no agenda, programming for every demographic, a focus on education and mentorship so communities produce their own leaders, equal space and programming for women, a welcoming space for everyone regardless of background or sect, an organization that unites and advertises other centres because institutions are vehicles without ego, empowerment of people and especially youth, genuine service rather than control, and getting closer to Allah together. In the second khutbah he explains that he himself gave covenants to his teachers to spread what he learned, that attending Jumuah makes the listeners party to the covenant too, and that in six or seven weeks he will write a contract for people to sign, because the ummah of 2060 is the sum of today's collective effort, one person at a time.

outline.heading: Opening
No communication during the khutbah
outline.gist: During the khutbah you may communicate only with Allah or with the khatib, unless lives depend on your response. Even he waits until after the khutbah to answer a page from the hospital.

outline.heading: Rereading the 2022 opening khutbah
outline.gist: He reads from his phone the khutbah he gave when the centre opened on February 18, 2022, the start of a series he calls our communal covenant.

outline.heading: We do not know what we owe each other
outline.gist: Without an agreement between those responsible for religious leadership and those who consume what they offer, communities run in circles like headless chickens. Today he gives his team's end of the bargain.

outline.heading: Surah Al-Jumu'ah as a statement of mutual duties
outline.gist: The verses on dropping trade at the call and not leaving the Prophet standing explain what each side owes. Any community needs a memorandum of understanding.

outline.heading: Neither side keeps its end of the bargain
outline.gist: Working in masajid around the world since age five, he has rarely seen them keep their side, and people do not keep theirs either, so the same problems recur.

outline.heading: The Prophet moved a society in 23 years
outline.gist: The society he left was not the one he was born into. Most of us have had longer, so something is missing, which is why the Prophet secured a covenant with the people of Madinah before migrating.

outline.heading: Not a bay'ah but a shared understanding
outline.gist: He asks for an understood covenant, not a pledge. Everyone shoulders weight by stage of life: the young are prepared and empowered, the elderly cherished and revered.

outline.heading: Shouldering or sitting on top?
outline.gist: Studying, marrying and working are not a contribution to the community. Ask what weight you carry, or whether others are carrying yours.

outline.heading: Point 1: balanced teaching with no agenda
outline.gist: Beneficial, relevant teaching that builds identity and confidence. He has no imam to promote, no one to make people hate and no group, only an objective reading of what Allah and the Prophet want.

outline.heading: Point 2: programming for every demographic
outline.gist: Programming for every age, background and level, from beginners to academic learners, expanding as space and funding allow.

outline.heading: Point 3: education and mentorship
outline.gist: No centre can do everything; this one focuses on teaching across the Islamic disciplines and mentoring the young so communities produce their own leaders instead of flying in speakers who do not understand them.

outline.heading: Who knows where Allah sends you
outline.gist: In 2010 he would have laughed at anyone saying he would stand in London, Ontario, since he never meant to leave Syria. Mentorship prepares people to serve wherever they land.

outline.heading: Point 4: space and programming for sisters
outline.gist: Both genders learn, with dedicated sisters' programming even at the cost of his own. The segregation he grew up with does not work in the West, where excluded daughters feel shut out.

outline.heading: Point 5: a welcoming space for everyone
outline.gist: No one, of any background or sect, is frowned upon, because it is Allah's house and those who run it welcome His guests on His behalf.

outline.heading: Turned away over jeans or a tattoo
outline.gist: People scolded for their jeans, a tattoo or a hat never come back, and if not welcome here they find somewhere worse.

outline.heading: Point 6: an organization that unites
outline.gist: In his years at two London masajid none ever advertised another's programs; in its first week this centre printed the whole city's agenda.

outline.heading: Institutions are vehicles without ego
outline.gist: An institution is a car to get somewhere; when it stops working you get out. One that must be defended or would sacrifice someone for its survival is personal ego in disguise and should be dismantled.

outline.heading: Point 7: empowering people, as he was at 15
outline.gist: Empower people with ideas and skills, especially the youth. People let him learn, teach and take positions he did not deserve, while supervising and protecting him, as the Prophet did with his companions.

outline.heading: Be the bridge the young step on
outline.gist: See young people for what they can become. If your body or your ego has to be their stepping stone, so be it: we will be gone soon, and without empowered youth the ummah has no better future than recent years.

outline.heading: Point 9: service, not control
outline.gist: Khidmah is a core ethic. He is not here to control anyone or push his opinions; he wants people to think and reach conclusions they can stand by, since control belongs to Allah. He is an abd, and an abd serves.

outline.heading: Point 10: getting closer to Allah together
outline.gist: The last commitment is to bring everyone closer to Allah together, loving Him more and bathing in His mercy, which matters more than anything else.

outline.heading: His end of the bargain
outline.gist: Balanced teaching with no agendas, a welcoming space, programming for every demographic and both genders, empowerment, teaching and mentorship.

outline.heading: Interlude
The opposite question
outline.gist: His team may find these commitments too much and leave. Over the coming weeks he will explain what the community offers in return.

outline.heading: His teachers' covenants
outline.gist: Five or six times a teacher took his hand and bound him to spread what he learned until he died. After the hours they spent on him, a covenant is the only fair return.

outline.heading: You are party to the covenant too
outline.gist: Coming to Jumuah makes you part of it. Part of the community's side is holding him accountable for what he promised; part is understanding what belonging to a community means.

outline.heading: A contract to sign, and the world of 2060
outline.gist: At the end of the series he will write a contract and sign it himself, since it is the least we owe one another. How the ummah looks in 2060 is the sum of what people decide now.

outline.heading: Add your little effort to the collective
outline.gist: If you dislike what is happening in Sudan, Yemen, Lebanon, Afghanistan, Iran or to Muslims in the West, add your small effort to the collective; no one can change the world alone.

outline.heading: One person at a time
outline.gist: The Prophet, given a mandate to reach everyone while even his uncle would not listen, was told to work one person at a time, and two billion Muslims must do the same. Teaching from the minbar is only a sliver of the work, so each must find a role.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.note: Communities stagnate because no understanding exists between those who run masajid and those who attend; a covenant where everyone shoulders some weight is the only way forward, and the ummah's future is the sum of collective effort.

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette

themes.label: Significance and etiquettes of Jumuah
themes.note: No phones or communication during the khutbah unless lives depend on your response; Surah Al-Jumu'ah itself describes what attendee and khatib owe each other.

themes.label: Methodology: how to read texts, tafsir method, intellectual approach
themes.note: He commits to teaching with no agenda or group affiliation, looking as objectively as possible at what the Prophet wanted and what Allah wants from us today.

themes.label: Education, schools and learning disorders
themes.note: Programming for every age, background and level, and a deliberate focus on teaching and mentorship so that communities raise their own speakers and leaders rather than importing them.

themes.label: Inclusion of women and sisters' programming in the masjid
themes.note: Equal learning space for sisters, with dedicated programming and a willingness to give up his own slots; the segregation he grew up with does not work in the West, where excluded daughters leave.

themes.label: Tolerance, pluralism and dealing with difference
themes.note: Everyone, of any background or sect, is welcome because the masjid is Allah's house and its people welcome His guests; those turned away find somewhere worse.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Institutional ego is personal ego hidden inside an institution; an institution that needs defending or would sacrifice someone for itself should be dismantled.

themes.label: Youth, their challenges and their role
themes.note: Empower young people with ideas and skills as he was empowered at 15 or 16; see their potential rather than their present, and let your body be the bridge they step on.

themes.label: Knowing Allah / relationship with Allah
themes.note: The tenth commitment: getting closer to Allah together, loving Him more and bathing in His mercy, which matters more than anything else.

themes.label: Oaths, promises, trust and loyalty
themes.note: His teachers took his hand and made him pledge to spread what they taught until he died; anyone attending Jumuah is already party to the covenant, and a written contract will be offered for signing.

themes.label: Accountability before Allah and goals
themes.note: Part of the community's role is to hold him accountable for delivering what he promised; if he provides nothing the whole system is corrupt.
